newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian investors cautious on new 30-year bond.
newsitem.headline: Austrian investors cautious on new 30-year bond.

text.p: Austria on Tuesday put on sale its first 30-year bond since World War Two, but the issue was met with scant interest as domestic investors remained cautious about taking on the risk, traders said.
"The timing is excellent (for the authorities) because we are at a historically low interest rate level but investors are afraid to take the rate risk for the next 30 years", said a trader.
"International investors have more experience with such a long maturity. Institutional investors here are in a wait-and-see position", he added.
Austria's Kontrollbank, the government's financing agent, earlier on Tuesday said it had issued the new stripped bond with a coupon of 6.25 percent and a maximum yield of 6.45 percent.
Austria followed the examples of Germany, France and the Netherlands which all have issued 30-year bonds recently. The longest maturity of an Austrian bond so far has been 18 years.

"We believe that we have to offer investors this segment", Helmut Eder, the head of the Austrian state financing agency, told Reuters, adding the issue was aimed at making Vienna a more attractive market for international investors.
Peter Brezinschek, an analyst at Raiffeisen Zentralbank, said the new 30-year bond was "basically a very interesting instrument".

"It was important to prolong the maturity pattern while offering to lower the risk by stripping off the coupons", he said, adding that European 30-year bonds were set to compete with U.S. Treasuries in the longer term. -- Christian Gutlederer, Vienna Newsroom, +43 1 53112-275
